summary: Bootstraps Homebrew at the default `/opt/homebrew` prefix, reserved for auxiliary CLIs (jq, git, gh) and GUI casks only — the primary language runtimes ship their own brew-free installers. Update runs `brew update` to refresh Homebrew and its formula definitions.
manualSteps: On a fresh Mac, creating `/opt/homebrew` needs administrator rights. Because `NONINTERACTIVE=1` suppresses the password prompt and this app runs commands without a terminal, run the very first bootstrap yourself in Terminal.app: paste the official command from https://brew.sh (it will ask for your admin password). Once `/opt/homebrew` exists and is owned by your account, this app's Update and later brew operations need no sudo.

Keep the default `/opt/homebrew` prefix — a custom prefix loses access to precompiled bottles and forces slow from-source builds for most formulae. If you want it to appear under a custom apps folder, symlink rather than relocate.

Per product policy, use Homebrew only for auxiliary tools (jq, git, gh) and GUI casks (VS Code, Cursor), not for the primary language/runtime recipes — those install brew-free so your toolchains stay independent of Homebrew.

summary: Installs Node.js through nvm into a relocated `NVM_DIR` at `$DEV_HOME/js/nvm` (instead of the default `~/.nvm`). Update runs `nvm install --lts` and repoints the `default` alias, keeping you on the latest LTS Node.
updateCommand: export NVM_DIR="$DEV_HOME/js/nvm" && source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" && nvm install --lts && nvm alias default 'lts/*'
manualSteps: nvm is a shell function sourced from `nvm.sh`, not a binary on `PATH` (PRD §9.7), so this app drives it through an interactive shell (`zsh -ic`). Shell startup banners may leak into the log output — that is expected and safe to ignore.

Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc`. Then add `source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh"` after them so `nvm`, `node`, and `npm` resolve in every new terminal you open.
Several other recipes (Codex CLI, opencode) run their npm installs through this nvm-managed Node, so install this recipe first if you plan to use them.

summary: The npm package manager that ships with the nvm-managed Node.js. Update upgrades npm itself inside the active default Node; the download cache lives at `~/.npm`.
detectCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" >/dev/null 2>&1 && { nvm use default || nvm use node; } >/dev/null 2>&1 && command -v npm >/dev/null 2>&1
currentVersionCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" >/dev/null 2>&1 && { nvm use default || nvm use node; } >/dev/null 2>&1 && npm --version
updateCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" && { nvm use default || nvm use node; } && npm install -g npm@latest
manualSteps: npm ships with Node.js — install the Node.js (nvm) recipe first; there is nothing separate to install here.
Update runs `npm install -g npm@latest` inside the nvm default Node, so it only affects the currently selected Node version.

summary: Installs the pnpm package manager to a managed `PNPM_HOME` at `$DEV_HOME/js/pnpm` via pnpm's official standalone script. Update re-runs the same script, which upgrades pnpm in place.
manualSteps: Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc`. Then put `PNPM_HOME` on your `PATH` with `export PATH="$PNPM_HOME:$PATH"` so the `pnpm` command resolves in your own terminals.
pnpm is installed as a standalone binary and does not need Node to run itself. To install Node too, use the Node.js (nvm) recipe, or run `pnpm env use --global lts` after pnpm is on your PATH.

summary: Installs the Bun JavaScript runtime, bundler, and package manager under a managed `BUN_INSTALL` at `$DEV_HOME/js/bun` via Bun's official script. Update runs `bun upgrade`, which replaces the binary in place with the latest release.
manualSteps: Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc`. Then add Bun to your `PATH` with `export PATH="$BUN_INSTALL/bin:$PATH"` so the `bun` command resolves in your own terminals.
Bun's installer normally edits your shell profile automatically; because this recipe runs non-interactively, add the export and PATH lines yourself as above.

summary: Installs a Java toolchain through SDKMAN into a relocated `SDKMAN_DIR` at `$DEV_HOME/java/sdkman`, configured to answer prompts automatically; the Gradle cache lives at `$DEV_HOME/java/gradle` (`GRADLE_USER_HOME`), shared with the Android SDK recipe. Update runs `sdk install java` to fetch the latest Java release.
currentVersionCommand: export SDKMAN_DIR="$DEV_HOME/java/sdkman" && source "$SDKMAN_DIR/bin/sdkman-init.sh" && sdk current java
installCommand: export SDKMAN_DIR="$DEV_HOME/java/sdkman" && curl -s https://get.sdkman.io | bash && sed -i '' 's/sdkman_auto_answer=false/sdkman_auto_answer=true/' "$SDKMAN_DIR/etc/config" && source "$SDKMAN_DIR/bin/sdkman-init.sh" && sdk install java
updateCommand: export SDKMAN_DIR="$DEV_HOME/java/sdkman" && sed -i '' 's/sdkman_auto_answer=false/sdkman_auto_answer=true/' "$SDKMAN_DIR/etc/config" && source "$SDKMAN_DIR/bin/sdkman-init.sh" && sdk install java
manualSteps: `sdk` is a shell function sourced from `sdkman-init.sh`, not a binary on `PATH` (PRD §9.7), so this app drives it through an interactive shell (`zsh -ic`); expect shell startup banners in the log output.

Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc`. Then add `source "$SDKMAN_DIR/bin/sdkman-init.sh"` after them so `sdk` and `java` resolve in every new terminal.
`GRADLE_USER_HOME` (`$DEV_HOME/java/gradle`) is shared with the Android SDK recipe so the Gradle cache is counted once, not twice — leave it in place if you use both.

externalCandidates.label: ~/.sdkman (default SDKMAN_DIR)
externalCandidates.currentVersionCommand: export SDKMAN_DIR="$HOME/.sdkman" && source "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh" && sdk current java

summary: Installs the Rust toolchain via rustup with `RUSTUP_HOME` and `CARGO_HOME` relocated to `$DEV_HOME/rust/rustup` and `$DEV_HOME/rust/cargo` (installed with `--no-modify-path`, so your shell profile is left untouched). Update runs `rustup update` to refresh the stable toolchain.
manualSteps: The installer runs with `--no-modify-path`, so wire the toolchain into your shell yourself: click the "Copy export lines" button in this recipe's detail view, paste them into `~/.zshrc`, and add `export PATH="$CARGO_HOME/bin:$PATH"` so `cargo`, `rustc`, and `rustup` resolve in your own terminals.
Building crates needs the Xcode Command Line Tools' linker. If a build fails with a missing linker or compiler, run `xcode-select --install` (a GUI prompt appears) and retry.

summary: Installs a current Go toolchain from go.dev's official tarball into `$DEV_HOME/go/toolchain` (with `GOPATH` at `$DEV_HOME/go/gopath`) and sets `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` so Go switches per-project versions from `go.mod` on its own. Update re-downloads and extracts the latest release, replacing the toolchain in place.
manualSteps: Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc`. Then add the toolchain to your `PATH` with `export PATH="$DEV_HOME/go/toolchain/go/bin:$GOPATH/bin:$PATH"` so the `go` command resolves in your own terminals.

This recipe supports pinning a specific Go version in the detail view; leave it empty to always fetch the latest. Because `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` is set, a project's `go.mod` can still pull a different toolchain automatically when you build it.

summary: CPython interpreters managed by uv, installed under `$DEV_HOME/python/uv/pythons`. Install fetches the latest stable CPython; per-project versions are handled by uv (`.python-version`, `uv python pin`).
manualSteps: Install the uv recipe first — this recipe installs and updates CPython through `uv python install`.
Never use the macOS system `/usr/bin/python3` for development — it is an Xcode Command Line Tools shim, not a full interpreter (PRD §9.6).
To make these interpreters available in your terminal and projects, use uv (`uv run`, `uv venv`, `uv python pin <version>`) rather than putting the interpreter on PATH by hand.

summary: Installs Astral's uv Python package/version manager with every data directory relocated under `$DEV_HOME/python/uv` — the `uv`/`uvx` binaries, cache, installed tools, and downloaded Python interpreters. Update runs `uv self update` to upgrade uv in place.
manualSteps: Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc`. Then add uv to your `PATH` with `export PATH="$UV_INSTALL_DIR:$UV_TOOL_BIN_DIR:$PATH"` so `uv`, `uvx`, and any tools you install with `uv tool install` resolve in your own terminals.

uv manages its own downloaded interpreters under `$DEV_HOME/python/uv/pythons`. Don't rely on the system `/usr/bin/python3`, which is an Xcode Command Line Tools stub, not a real development interpreter (PRD §9.6).

summary: The pip package installer inside the uv-managed CPython, for tools and workflows that still expect plain pip. Day-to-day dependency management is better served by uv itself (`uv add`, `uv pip`).
updateCommand: PYBIN="$(ls -d "$UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR"/*/bin/python3 2>/dev/null | sort | tail -1)" && "$PYBIN" -m pip install --upgrade pip
manualSteps: Install the Python recipe first — pip is bootstrapped into the newest uv-managed CPython with `ensurepip`.
Prefer uv for real dependency work (`uv add`, `uv pip install`); keep pip for tools that call it directly.

summary: Installs the rbenv Ruby version manager by cloning it directly from GitHub into `$DEV_HOME/ruby/rbenv` (avoiding the official installer's silent Homebrew fallback). Update pulls the latest rbenv/ruby-build, then compiles and selects the newest stable Ruby as your global version.
installCommand: mkdir -p "$DEV_HOME/ruby" && git clone https://github.com/rbenv/rbenv.git "${RBENV_ROOT:?}" && git clone https://github.com/rbenv/ruby-build.git "$RBENV_ROOT/plugins/ruby-build"
updateCommand: git -C "${RBENV_ROOT:?}" pull --ff-only && git -C "$RBENV_ROOT/plugins/ruby-build" pull --ff-only && LATEST_RUBY="$("$RBENV_ROOT/bin/rbenv" install -l 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^[[:space:]]*[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$' | tail -1 | tr -d '[:space:]')" && "$RBENV_ROOT/bin/rbenv" install -s "$LATEST_RUBY" && "$RBENV_ROOT/bin/rbenv" global "$LATEST_RUBY" && "$RBENV_ROOT/bin/rbenv" rehash
manualSteps: Install sets up the version manager only (like the Node.js (nvm) recipe). Press Update to compile and select the latest stable Ruby — this can take several minutes and is streamed live in the log.
Compiling Ruby with ruby-build needs the Xcode Command Line Tools. If the build reports a missing compiler, run `xcode-select --install` (a GUI prompt appears) and retry Update.

ruby-build on macOS has historically needed OpenSSL/readline libraries that Homebrew usually supplies. Under the no-brew policy this is a known tension: if the Ruby build fails on OpenSSL, provide those libraries (or accept using Homebrew for just that dependency) and update again.

Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc`. Then add `export PATH="$RBENV_ROOT/bin:$PATH"` and `eval "$(rbenv init - zsh)"` so `rbenv` and your selected Ruby resolve in your own terminals.

summary: Installs CocoaPods as a gem into the rbenv-managed Ruby, with its repos/templates directory relocated via `CP_HOME_DIR` to `$DEV_HOME/ruby/cocoapods`. Update runs `gem update cocoapods` and rehashes rbenv's shims.
installCommand: mkdir -p "$CP_HOME_DIR" && "$RBENV_ROOT/bin/rbenv" exec gem install cocoapods && "$RBENV_ROOT/bin/rbenv" rehash
uninstallCommand: "$RBENV_ROOT/bin/rbenv" exec gem uninstall -aIx cocoapods 2>/dev/null; "$RBENV_ROOT/bin/rbenv" rehash 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "${CP_HOME_DIR:?}" "${HOME:?}/Library/Caches/CocoaPods"
manualSteps: Install the Ruby (rbenv) recipe and press Update on it first so a real Ruby exists. Otherwise `gem install cocoapods` targets the macOS system Ruby, which needs sudo and is discouraged.

`CP_HOME_DIR` relocates the CocoaPods repos/templates directory, but the separate download cache at `~/Library/Caches/CocoaPods` has not always honored `CP_HOME_DIR` across versions (PRD §9.8); it is tracked here as a best-effort disk path and removed on uninstall.

Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc` so `CP_HOME_DIR` and `RBENV_ROOT` match in your terminals. Run pod via `rbenv exec pod …` (or after `rbenv init`) so it uses the managed Ruby rather than the system one.

externalCandidates.label: pod on PATH (system gem or Homebrew)

summary: Prepares the `ANDROID_HOME` folder at `$DEV_HOME/android/sdk` and the shared Gradle cache (`$DEV_HOME/java/gradle`); the SDK components themselves are downloaded by Android Studio's first-run wizard, the only step that can set the SDK path. There is no automated update — SDK components are managed from Android Studio's SDK Manager.
manualSteps: Download and install Android Studio from https://developer.android.com/studio (a GUI app; not scriptable here).

In Android Studio's first-run Setup Wizard, choose Custom setup and set the Android SDK Location to the prepared path `$DEV_HOME/android/sdk`. This path cannot be scripted — it must be typed into the wizard (PRD §9.8).

Accept the SDK license agreements so the wizard downloads platform-tools, an SDK Platform, and build-tools into that folder. Until then the recipe shows the folder as present but reports no `adb` version.

Install component updates later via Android Studio → Settings → Languages & Frameworks → Android SDK (the SDK Manager). The Gradle cache at `$DEV_HOME/java/gradle` is shared with the Java (SDKMAN) recipe and is left untouched on uninstall.

Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc`. Then add the platform tools to your `PATH` with `export PATH="$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools:$PATH"` so `adb` and other SDK tools resolve in your own terminals.

summary: Installs Docker Desktop by downloading the official DMG for Apple Silicon and copying `Docker.app` into `/Applications`; the first launch (privileged helper, license) is inherently manual. Update re-downloads the latest DMG and cleanly replaces the existing app bundle.
installCommand: hdiutil detach "$TMPDIR/lazyenv-docker-mnt" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "${TMPDIR:?}/lazyenv-docker-mnt"; mkdir -p "$TMPDIR/lazyenv-docker-mnt" && curl -fSL https://desktop.docker.com/mac/main/arm64/Docker.dmg -o "$TMPDIR/Docker.dmg" && hdiutil attach "$TMPDIR/Docker.dmg" -nobrowse -mountpoint "$TMPDIR/lazyenv-docker-mnt" && ditto "$TMPDIR/lazyenv-docker-mnt/Docker.app" /Applications/Docker.app && hdiutil detach "$TMPDIR/lazyenv-docker-mnt" && rm -f "${TMPDIR:?}/Docker.dmg"
updateCommand: hdiutil detach "$TMPDIR/lazyenv-docker-mnt" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "${TMPDIR:?}/lazyenv-docker-mnt" "${TMPDIR:?}/Docker.app.new"; mkdir -p "$TMPDIR/lazyenv-docker-mnt" && curl -fSL https://desktop.docker.com/mac/main/arm64/Docker.dmg -o "$TMPDIR/Docker.dmg" && hdiutil attach "$TMPDIR/Docker.dmg" -nobrowse -mountpoint "$TMPDIR/lazyenv-docker-mnt" && ditto "$TMPDIR/lazyenv-docker-mnt/Docker.app" "$TMPDIR/Docker.app.new" && hdiutil detach "$TMPDIR/lazyenv-docker-mnt" && rm -rf /Applications/Docker.app && ditto "$TMPDIR/Docker.app.new" /Applications/Docker.app && rm -rf "${TMPDIR:?}/Docker.app.new" && rm -f "${TMPDIR:?}/Docker.dmg"
manualSteps: First launch is manual: open Docker Desktop from `/Applications`. It installs a privileged helper (macOS prompts for your password) and asks you to accept the service agreement — the app cannot script past these OS-level prompts (PRD §9.10).

Copying `Docker.app` into `/Applications` assumes your account is an administrator (the app cannot supply a sudo password). If the copy is denied, open the downloaded DMG and drag `Docker.app` to Applications yourself.
Before running Update, quit Docker Desktop so its app bundle can be replaced cleanly — Update removes the old `/Applications/Docker.app` and copies the new version in (a clean replace, not a merge).
Docker's disk-image/data location is configurable only in Docker Desktop → Settings → Resources → Advanced, not from here (PRD §9.10).

summary: Installs Neovim from the latest official GitHub release tarball for Apple Silicon into `$DEV_HOME/tools/neovim`. Update re-fetches the newest release tag and replaces the extracted build in place.
manualSteps: The `nvim` binary lands at `$DEV_HOME/tools/neovim/nvim-macos-arm64/bin/nvim`, which isn't on your `PATH` by default. Add `export PATH="$DEV_HOME/tools/neovim/nvim-macos-arm64/bin:$PATH"` to `~/.zshrc` so the `nvim` command works in your own terminals.
Install this recipe before LunarVim — LunarVim requires Neovim 0.9+ and will not install Neovim itself.

summary: Installs LunarVim from its Neovim-compatibility release branch (`release-1.4/neovim-0.9`) into `~/.local/share/lunarvim`, with the `lvim` launcher placed at `~/.local/bin`. Update re-runs the same pinned installer; because the branch URL drifts as new Neovim versions ship, it is tracked with `lastVerified` and should be checked periodically (PRD §9.9).
manualSteps: Install the Neovim recipe first — LunarVim's installer requires Neovim 0.9+ and will not install Neovim itself (on macOS it only prints a `brew install neovim` suggestion and exits, PRD §9.9).

Optional language-server dependencies are installed only if `node`/`npm`, `python`, or `cargo` are already on `PATH`; otherwise the installer skips them with a warning (safe to add later once those recipes are installed).

Add `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` to `~/.zshrc` so the `lvim` command resolves. Note the pinned installer branch can go stale as Neovim advances — if an install fails, check the recipe's `lastVerified` date and confirm the branch URL is still current (PRD §9.9).

summary: Relocates Xcode's DerivedData build cache to `$DEV_HOME/xcode/derived-data` via Xcode's official `IDECustomDerivedDataLocation` setting (`defaults write com.apple.dt.Xcode`), the Apple-supported alternative to symlinking. Re-run Relocate to re-apply the setting if it is ever reset.
manualSteps: Quit and relaunch Xcode so it picks up the new DerivedData location. The old `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData` folder is safe to delete manually; Xcode regenerates build data on the next build.
You can verify or change this in Xcode → Settings → Locations → Derived Data, which edits the same `IDECustomDerivedDataLocation` preference this recipe writes.

summary: Moves Xcode's Archives, iOS/watchOS DeviceSupport, and the SwiftPM cache into `$DEV_HOME/xcode` using an idempotent move-then-symlink (no official relocation exists for these). Quit Xcode before running; re-run Relocate safely anytime — already-linked folders are skipped.
installCommand: reloc() { s="$1"; d="$2"; [ -L "$s" ] && return 0; if [ -e "$s" ] && [ -e "$d" ]; then echo "xcode-dev-caches: [$s] and its destination [$d] both contain data; consolidate into one and remove the other, then re-run" >&2; return 1; fi; mkdir -p "$(dirname "$d")"; if [ -e "$s" ]; then mv "$s" "$d"; else mkdir -p "$d"; fi; mkdir -p "$(dirname "$s")"; ln -s "$d" "$s"; }; reloc "$HOME/Library/Developer/Xcode/Archives" "$DEV_HOME/xcode/Archives" && reloc "$HOME/Library/Developer/Xcode/iOS DeviceSupport" "$DEV_HOME/xcode/iOS DeviceSupport" && reloc "$HOME/Library/Developer/Xcode/watchOS DeviceSupport" "$DEV_HOME/xcode/watchOS DeviceSupport" && reloc "$HOME/Library/Caches/org.swift.swiftpm" "$DEV_HOME/xcode/org.swift.swiftpm"
manualSteps: Quit Xcode before running this — Xcode must not be writing to these folders during the move.

Symlinks are created even for DeviceSupport folders that don't exist yet, so future device-support data also lands in the managed location. Already-symlinked folders are skipped, so re-running is safe (idempotent).

If a folder exists in BOTH the original location and the managed destination (e.g. from a previous partial run), the relocate stops with a 'conflict' message instead of overwriting either copy — merge the two into one and delete the other, then run again.

summary: Reclaims Simulator disk space by deleting unavailable simulator devices via the supported `xcrun simctl delete unavailable` command; usage is measured under `~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator`. Runtime-image deletion is a separate manual `simctl` step because the images are SIP-protected and cannot be moved, symlinked, or `rm`'d (PRD §9.5).
manualSteps: To reclaim the large simulator runtime images (multiple GB each), list installed runtimes with `xcrun simctl runtime list`, then delete a specific one with `xcrun simctl runtime delete <identifier>`. These images live under `/System/Library/AssetsV2` (SIP-protected) and can only be removed through simctl — never with `rm`, symlinks, or a relocation (PRD §9.5).

Do not try to relocate `~/Library/Developer/CoreSimulator/Devices` to another volume — CoreSimulator's daemon has real-world reports of breaking when that data is symlinked, so this recipe only cleans up rather than moves (PRD §9.5).

summary: Installs Claude Code via Anthropic's official native installer (`claude.ai/install.sh`, not the deprecated npm package) to `~/.local/bin/claude`, with its config directory relocated via `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` to `$DEV_HOME/ai/claude`. Update re-runs the native installer to fetch the latest stable build; credentials stay in the macOS Keychain.
installCommand: set -o pipefail && curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash -s stable
updateCommand: set -o pipefail && curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash -s stable
manualSteps: First run requires interactive sign-in — launch `claude` in a terminal to authenticate (browser OAuth or API key). Credentials are stored in the macOS Keychain and are not managed or removed by this recipe.

Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc` so `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` matches in your terminals. Also add `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` so the `claude` command resolves in your own shells.

externalCandidates.label: claude on PATH (npm or other), default ~/.claude config

summary: Installs OpenAI's Codex CLI globally via npm (`@openai/codex`) using nvm's default Node, with its config directory relocated via `CODEX_HOME` to `$DEV_HOME/ai/codex`. It uses the scoped package name — the unscoped `codex` npm package is an unrelated project (PRD §9.12). Update reinstalls the latest version. Requires the Node.js (nvm) recipe first.
detectCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" && nvm use default >/dev/null 2>&1 && command -v codex >/dev/null 2>&1
installCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" && nvm use default && npm install -g @openai/codex
updateCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" && nvm use default && npm install -g @openai/codex@latest
uninstallCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" && nvm use default >/dev/null 2>&1 && npm uninstall -g @openai/codex; rm -rf "${CODEX_HOME:?}"
manualSteps: Install the Node.js (nvm) recipe first — this uses nvm's default Node to run npm.
Only the scoped package `@openai/codex` is correct; do not install the unscoped `codex` npm package, which is a different, unrelated tool (PRD §9.12).

Open this recipe's detail view, click the "Copy export lines" button, and paste them into `~/.zshrc` so `CODEX_HOME` matches in your terminals. Because it installs through nvm's Node, make sure your shell sources `nvm.sh` (see the Node.js (nvm) recipe) so the `codex` command resolves.

summary: Installs the opencode AI coding agent globally via npm (`opencode-ai`) using nvm's default Node. It follows the XDG base-directory spec natively (config at `~/.config/opencode`, data at `~/.local/share/opencode`), so no env overrides are needed — the simplest of the three agents. Update reinstalls the latest version. Requires the Node.js (nvm) recipe first.
detectCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" && nvm use default >/dev/null 2>&1 && command -v opencode >/dev/null 2>&1
installCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" && nvm use default && npm install -g opencode-ai
updateCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" && nvm use default && npm install -g opencode-ai@latest
uninstallCommand: source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh" && nvm use default >/dev/null 2>&1 && npm uninstall -g opencode-ai; rm -rf "${HOME:?}/.config/opencode" "${HOME:?}/.local/share/opencode"
manualSteps: Install the Node.js (nvm) recipe first — this uses nvm's default Node to run npm.

opencode needs no dedicated env vars — it reads `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`/`XDG_DATA_HOME` if you set them, otherwise the standard `~/.config` and `~/.local/share` locations. Ensure your shell sources `nvm.sh` (see the Node.js (nvm) recipe) so the globally installed `opencode` command resolves.
